lessons.title: Autumn Starter
lessons.description:
In this Autumn Starter lesson, students revise a range of English skills through grammar, comprehension, spelling, punctuation and writing activities.

This lesson includes:
✔ Using standard verb forms correctly
✔ Mixed comprehension and prediction skills
✔ Practising statutory spelling words
✔ Using apostrophes for plural possession
✔ Fronted adverbials and prepositions
✔ Correctly punctuating direct speech
✔ Using subordinating conjunctions

Students begin by identifying incorrect verb forms and correcting sentences using standard English, including choosing accurately between forms such as did and done, saw and seen, and was and were.

The reading activity follows Rishabh as he discovers an old book called The Mystery of the Moon. Students retrieve information, use contextual clues, identify vocabulary and make predictions based on evidence from the text.

Students then practise statutory spelling words including breath, library, remember, arrive, potatoes, special and through, using selected letters to reveal the hidden word harvest.

The punctuation section focuses on apostrophes for plural possession. Students identify where apostrophes belong in examples such as the squirrels’ acorns, the badgers’ set, the trees’ berries, the foxes’ digging and the moles’ hills.

Finally, students apply a mixture of punctuation, grammar and vocabulary skills to picture-based writing. They construct sentences containing a fronted adverbial, a preposition, correctly punctuated direct speech and a subordinating conjunction.

By the end of the lesson, students will have revised and applied a broad range of Year 4 English skills involving grammar, reading comprehension, spelling, punctuation and sentence construction.

lessons.title: Prepositions, Adverbial Phrases
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of prepositions and adverbial phrases. They learn how prepositions describe place, time and movement, identify prepositions within sentences and passages, and distinguish between prepositions and subordinating conjunctions. Students then explore how adverbial phrases add information about how, when, where, why and for how long an action happens.

This lesson includes:
✔ Identifying prepositions of place, time and movement
✔ Using prepositions accurately in sentences
✔ Distinguishing prepositions from other word classes
✔ Recognising when words such as after and since act as prepositions or subordinating conjunctions
✔ Identifying and using adverbial phrases

Students begin by exploring what prepositions are and how they describe relationships involving place, time and movement.

Students will:
✔ Identify common prepositions
✔ Describe the position of objects using prepositions
✔ Sort prepositions from other word classes
✔ Recognise prepositional phrases
✔ Use appropriate prepositions to complete sentences

Students then apply their understanding by creating sentences from pictures and identifying prepositions within longer passages.

Students will:
✔ Use prepositions of location accurately
✔ Use prepositions of time accurately
✔ Use prepositions of movement and direction
✔ Replace prepositions while maintaining grammatical sentences
✔ Explain how changing a preposition changes meaning

The lesson also explores words that can function as either prepositions or subordinating conjunctions depending on their grammatical context.

Students will:
✔ Examine words such as after, before, until, as and since
✔ Identify whether a word introduces a noun phrase or a subordinate clause
✔ Distinguish prepositions from subordinating conjunctions
✔ Use surrounding sentence structure to determine grammatical function

The lesson then introduces adverbial phrases and explores the additional information they provide within sentences.

Students will:
✔ Identify adverbial phrases in sentences
✔ Recognise adverbials describing how an action happens
✔ Identify adverbials of time and frequency
✔ Recognise adverbials describing place
✔ Identify phrases explaining why or for how long something happens

Students practise identifying examples such as 'in a rush', 'at once', 'every day', 'this morning', 'since Wednesday', 'almost always', 'with a limp', 'like a snake', 'one by one' and 'in a line'.

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently identify and use prepositions of place, time and movement, distinguish prepositions from subordinating conjunctions, and recognise how adverbial phrases provide additional information about actions and events.

lessons.title: Present perfect tense
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of the present perfect tense and learn how it differs from the simple past tense. They explore how the present perfect connects actions or events from the past to the present and practise forming it correctly using has or have with the past participle of a verb.

This lesson includes:
✔ Recognising the present perfect tense
✔ Distinguishing between simple past and present perfect tense
✔ Using has and have correctly
✔ Understanding past participles
✔ Converting past tense sentences into the present perfect
✔ Identifying regular and irregular verb forms
✔ Choosing the correct tense according to context and meaning
✔ Using present perfect forms accurately in sentences

Students begin by learning how sentences can be changed from the past tense into the present perfect tense using has or have with the appropriate verb form. They explore examples such as 'the alien won' becoming 'the alien has won' and 'the aliens landed' becoming 'the aliens have landed'.

Students also learn that the present perfect can describe something that began in the past and is still continuing in the present. For example, 'Timmy has been in his spaceship for twenty years' tells us that Timmy entered the spaceship in the past and remains there now.

Students will:
✔ Convert past tense verbs into present perfect forms
✔ Use have with I, you, we and they
✔ Use has with he, she and it
✔ Recognise common irregular forms such as grown, done, eaten, broken, gone, fallen and seen
✔ Create their own past tense and present perfect sentences

The lesson provides extensive practice with regular and irregular verbs. Students compare forms such as ate and have eaten, broke and has broken, went and have gone, fell and have fallen, and saw and have seen.

Students then compare sentences in the simple past and present perfect tenses and learn how timing affects which form should be used. The simple past is used for actions or events that started and finished in the past, whereas the present perfect is used when an earlier action is still true, continues into the present or has an effect on what is happening now.

Further activities involve matching past tense sentences with their present perfect equivalents, rewriting a football match recount in the present perfect tense, identifying the tense used in sentences and selecting the most appropriate verb form according to context.

Students also learn that the present perfect uses the auxiliary verb have or has followed by the past participle, or third form, of the main verb. They practise choosing accurate forms such as has grown rather than has grew, have done rather than have did, has come rather than has came, and have forgotten rather than have forgot.

By the end of the lesson, students will confidently distinguish between the simple past and present perfect tenses, use has and have correctly, select appropriate past participles and understand when a past action remains connected to the present.

lessons.title: Prefixes
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of prefixes and how adding a prefix to the beginning of a root word can create a new word and change its meaning. The lesson focuses particularly on the prefixes super, auto and anti. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding what a prefix is
✔ Exploring the meanings of super, auto and anti
✔ Using prefixes to create new words
✔ Using word meanings to identify the correct prefix
✔ Working out the meanings of unfamiliar prefixed words
✔ Matching prefixes with appropriate root words
✔ Using prefixed words accurately in sentences
✔ Applying grammar and punctuation skills in a short writing task

Students begin by learning that a prefix is a group of letters added to the beginning of a word to create a new word. They explore examples such as supermarket, autograph and antifreeze.

Students then investigate the meanings of three important prefixes:
✔ super – meaning greater, more than or above
✔ auto – meaning self or own
✔ anti – meaning against or the opposite of :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

Students use these meanings to explore words such as supernatural, superhero, supernova, automatic, autograph, autobiography, antifreeze, antibiotic and antiseptic.

They then apply their knowledge to unfamiliar vocabulary, using prefixes as clues to work out word meanings. Activities include identifying words such as superpower, autopilot and antisocial, and selecting the correct prefix to create words such as autocue, antidote and superglue.

Students will:
✔ Choose an appropriate prefix for a root word
✔ Explain the meaning of the new word
✔ Use the new word in a sentence
✔ Match prefixes to root words to form recognised English words
✔ Distinguish between possible prefix choices according to meaning and context

Further practice includes creating and using words such as automobile, antiseptic, superstore, antiviral, superfood, antibacterial, superstar, antibiotic, anticlimax and supersonic.

Students also complete quizzes in which they select the correct prefixed word and add super, auto or anti to words within sentences to make the meaning correct.

The lesson finishes with a creative writing activity called 'Stairway to the Unknown'. Students write five sentences inspired by a photograph, including a prepositional phrase, the personal pronoun he, a possessive apostrophe, an adverb and a question sentence. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}

By the end of the lesson, students will confidently understand and use the prefixes super, auto and anti, use prefixes to build new words, and use their knowledge of prefixes to work out the meanings of unfamiliar vocabulary.

lessons.title: Descriptive writing
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their descriptive writing skills by exploring how carefully chosen vocabulary and figurative language can create vivid and engaging images for the reader.

This lesson includes:
✔ Using interesting and precise adjectives
✔ Choosing powerful verbs
✔ Using adverbs to describe actions
✔ Creating effective similes
✔ Using metaphors to build vivid imagery
✔ Recognising and creating alliteration
✔ Using personification to bring descriptions to life
✔ Developing and improving descriptive vocabulary
✔ Writing extended descriptive passages

Students begin by revising important word classes used in descriptive writing. They identify nouns and explore how adjectives can add detail and help the reader picture a person, place, animal or object more clearly.

Students are encouraged to move beyond simple adjectives such as big, nice, beautiful, small and old, replacing them with more precise and imaginative vocabulary such as enormous, stunning, tiny and ancient.

The lesson then explores verbs and adverbs. Students identify suitable action words for a scene and add carefully chosen adverbs to explain how those actions are taking place.

Students will:
✔ Identify nouns, adjectives, verbs and adverbs
✔ Select more ambitious vocabulary
✔ Match powerful verbs to nouns within a scene
✔ Add adverbs to give actions greater detail
✔ Use vocabulary choices to create clearer images for the reader

The lesson then introduces a range of descriptive writing devices. Students learn that similes compare one thing with another using words such as like or as, while metaphors describe something as though it actually is something else.

Students also explore alliteration, where nearby words begin with the same sound, and personification, where human characteristics or actions are given to something non-human.

Students will:
✔ Create original similes
✔ Develop effective metaphors
✔ Recognise and use alliteration
✔ Use personification to make settings feel alive
✔ Combine figurative language with carefully selected vocabulary

Students then bring these techniques together in an extended descriptive writing task based on a beach scene. They are encouraged to write at least two or three paragraphs containing interesting adjectives, powerful verbs, carefully selected adverbs, similes, metaphors, alliteration and personification.

Further activities require students to focus closely on one object, person or animal and create a detailed description of it. They also review their own vocabulary and use a thesaurus to improve weaker word choices.

Students then apply the same descriptive techniques to another setting, such as a town centre, a busy market or the first day of school.

The lesson finishes by analysing a short descriptive passage and identifying examples of verbs, adverbs, adjectives, personification, alliteration, metaphor and simile.

By the end of the lesson, students will confidently use a range of vocabulary and figurative language techniques to make their descriptive writing more vivid, imaginative and engaging.

lessons.title: Plurals and Pronouns
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of singular and plural nouns and explore how pronouns and alternative nouns can be used to avoid unnecessary repetition in writing.

This lesson includes:
✔ Understanding the difference between singular and plural nouns
✔ Forming regular plurals by adding s or es
✔ Applying plural rules to nouns ending in ch, sh, s, ss, x and z
✔ Forming plurals of nouns ending in y
✔ Recognising when y changes to ies
✔ Exploring nouns ending in f or fe that change to ves
✔ Recognising irregular plurals such as foot and feet
✔ Recognising nouns such as sheep that remain unchanged in the plural
✔ Understanding what pronouns are and how they replace nouns
✔ Identifying personal, possessive, relative and reflexive pronouns
✔ Using pronouns to avoid repetition
✔ Using alternative nouns to make writing smoother and more varied
✔ Identifying pronouns within sentences
✔ Rewriting repetitive sentences and passages
✔ Using pronouns clearly so the reader knows which noun they refer to
✔ Using demonstrative pronouns such as this, that, these and those

Students begin by learning the difference between singular and plural nouns and exploring the spelling rules used to change nouns from one to more than one. They practise adding s and es, changing consonant-plus-y endings to ies and exploring exceptions such as loaf becoming loaves, foot becoming feet and sheep remaining sheep.

The lesson then introduces pronouns as words that can take the place of nouns. Students explore a range of personal, possessive, relative and reflexive pronouns, including he, she, it, they, mine, yours, who, which, that, myself and themselves.

Students identify pronouns in sentences before replacing repeated nouns with suitable pronouns. They then improve increasingly challenging sentences and passages by combining pronouns with alternative nouns, learning that repetition should be reduced without making it unclear who or what a pronoun refers to.

Further activities require students to construct their own sentences using selected pronouns and alternative nouns. They apply these skills to different picture prompts involving visitors, tourists, swimmers and competitors.

The lesson finishes with a demonstrative pronouns quiz focusing on this, that, these and those. Students use singular and plural context to select the correct pronoun and complete each sentence accurately.

By the end of the lesson, learners will confidently form a range of regular and irregular plurals, recognise and use different types of pronouns, reduce unnecessary repetition and select appropriate demonstrative pronouns according to meaning and number.

lessons.title: Standard English and Compound Words
lessons.description:
In this lesson, students develop their understanding of Standard English and compound words, learning how to recognise and correct non-standard forms and how words can be combined to create compound nouns with new meanings.

This lesson includes:
✔ Recognising the difference between Standard and non-standard English
✔ Correcting non-standard verb forms and expressions
✔ Using was and were accurately
✔ Choosing correct past tense forms such as saw and did
✔ Using have correctly instead of expressions such as should of and could of
✔ Distinguishing between commonly confused words such as borrow and lend
✔ Avoiding double negatives and informal expressions in formal writing
✔ Editing sentences, conversations and passages into Standard English
✔ Understanding what compound nouns are
✔ Combining words to create compound nouns
✔ Recognising open, closed and hyphenated compound nouns
✔ Understanding how compound words can develop new meanings
✔ Exploring how spoken stress can affect meaning
✔ Forming plurals of compound nouns correctly
✔ Identifying the important word within a compound noun when forming plurals
✔ Creating new compound nouns and definitions
✔ Building compound words from pictures and word clues

Students begin by comparing Standard English with forms that may occur in informal or regional speech. They correct examples such as we was to we were, I done it to I did it, I seen him to I saw him and should of to should have. They also explore vocabulary choices such as borrow and lend, our and are, and those and them within Standard English sentences.

Students then apply these skills to increasingly challenging material, correcting non-standard English within individual sentences, conversations, advertisements and a longer written extract. They learn to identify inappropriate verb forms, slang, double negatives and other constructions and replace them with suitable Standard English alternatives.

The second part of the lesson introduces compound nouns. Students learn that two or more words can combine to create a noun and that compound nouns may be written as one word, as separate words or with hyphens. They explore examples including football, steam train, armrest, handful and mother-in-law and learn to check unfamiliar spellings when necessary.

Students investigate how combining words can change meaning, comparing examples such as greenhouse and green house, redhead and red head, boyfriend and boy friend, and homework. They also explore how stress in spoken English can help distinguish between different meanings.

The lesson then examines how compound nouns are made plural. Students learn to identify the most important element of the compound and practise examples including footballs, sheep dips, fathers-in-law, platefuls, cryptocurrencies and eyeliners.

Finally, students create their own compound nouns and complete a series of word and picture challenges involving familiar compounds such as snowman, armchair, teapot, starfish, bathroom, paintbrush, sandcastle, crossroads, moonlight, butterfly, popcorn, dragonfly, raincoat, sunflower, bookshelf and seesaw.

By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to recognise and use Standard English more accurately, correct common non-standard constructions, understand how compound nouns are formed and spelled, and confidently identify, create and pluralise a range of compound words.
